To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the test performance of deep networks first degrades, and then improves, as a function of their model size, (ii) the test performance degrades as a function of number of train samples and (iii) there is a regime in which doubling the number of training samples actually hurts performance.

(1) as we increase the model size, performance gets worse and then better, and (2) as we increase number of training epochs, performance gets worse, and then better, with the optimal number of epochs being proportional to the number of training samples

(i) as the model capacity increases, the test performance first gets worse, then gets better, and then gets worse again, and (ii) as the number of training samples increases, the test accuracy first increases, then decreases, and then increases again, and (iii) these phenomena are related and can be explained by a single complexity measure, namely the effective model complexity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the relationship between data and model complexity, and the resulting performance of deep neural networks.
understanding when and why overparameterized neural networks perform well, and what happens if we push them beyond their sweet spot.
understanding how the performance of modern deep learning models depends on the number of parameters in the model, the amount of training data, and the number of training steps.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
more data is better" only if we are in the "overparameterized" regime, which is the regime where the effective model complexity is smaller than the training data size.
The larger the model, the more training data, and the more epochs of training, the better the test error.
the more complex model and more train data, the worse performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the "bigger-is-better" mantra does not always hold in deep learning.
the double-descent phenomena is a fundamental phenomenon that occurs not just in the context of model size and train samples but also in the context of the number of train epochs.
the performance of a neural network can be better than the one with a larger model or more training samples, which is a surprising result.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many ways in which model size and data size can interact, and we need to better understand these interactions before we can fully understand the limits of deep learning
the traditional view of overfitting as an issue of model complexity alone is insufficient to explain the full picture of modern deep learning.

, in the presence of data, model size alone is insufficient to characterize the generalization performance of a model, and we need to consider the interaction of the number of samples and the model size.
